title: Site Work Is Where the Drawings Meet the Ground, and the Ground Gets a Vote
summary: Site work is the first irreversible spend on a project: survey control, the logistics plan, earthworks, dewatering, temporary works and utilities. Each rests on assumptions about ground and water that are only partly known. Learn the six systems, who owns each, and how to turn unknowns into priced, watched risks.
body:
Site work is the moment the project stops being paper. Everything after it is built on the control points, the ground level, the water level and the temporary structures you set in the first months, so mistakes here are paid for in every later trade.

Recall

Q. What does the building permit approve, and what does it not?

A. It approves the documents as submitted and reviewed for code compliance. It does not certify that the design is error-free or right for your brief; the licensed designers own the design.

Q. What is life-cycle cost?

A. The total cost of owning an element over its life, first cost plus energy, maintenance, repair and replacement, brought back to today's money.

Q. What is a means of egress?

A. The continuous, unobstructed path from any point in a building to a public way, made of the exit access, the exit and the exit discharge.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the design phase taught you to decide in the order decisions become irreversible. Site work is the first place those decisions become physical. A survey point set 50 millimetres off moves every column. A dewatering system that fails floods the excavation. A temporary wall that moves cracks the neighbour's building. Site work is often a small share of hard cost, but it carries a large share of the early schedule and a large share of the claims. Your control system has to be strongest exactly where the information is weakest.

The six systems of site work

In plain English: before a building can rise, someone has to know exactly where it goes, how to get people and materials in and out, how to move the earth, how to keep water out of the hole, how to hold the sides of the hole up, and how to connect water, power, sewer and drainage. Those are the six systems.

The professional names are survey control, the site logistics plan, earthworks, dewatering, temporary works and utilities. Each has an owner. Survey control belongs to a licensed land surveyor. The logistics plan belongs to the contractor, approved by you and often by the city. Earthworks follow the civil and geotechnical engineers' specifications. Dewatering and temporary works are usually designed by specialists engaged by the contractor, checked by the engineer of record and sometimes by an independent checker. Utilities are designed by the civil and building services engineers and approved by each utility.

Survey control: one truth for location

Survey control is a set of fixed reference points, horizontal positions and elevations, called benchmarks and control points, from which every part of the building is set out. The surveyor establishes them from the legal boundary survey and a recognised vertical datum, the reference surface from which elevations are measured.

The discipline is that there is only one control network, and everyone works from it. Worked example. A hypothetical site has two elevation references: the architect's drawings use the city datum, and an old topographic survey used an assumed site datum 0.3 metres different. If nobody reconciles them, the ground floor may be set 0.3 metres too low. On a site near a flood zone, that can put the floor below the design flood elevation, which may mean a failed inspection, a raised floor slab, regraded entrances and redesigned ramps. Reconciling the datums on day one is an afternoon of the surveyor's time. Discovering the error at the floor-level inspection can cost a hypothetical 500,000 dollars and two months.

So the first site instruction is: protect the control points, check them regularly, and require the surveyor to certify key elements, such as foundations, column lines and the ground floor level, against the drawings before the next trade covers them.

The logistics plan: a site is a factory with no roof

The site logistics plan shows how the site works during construction: gates and traffic routes, crane positions and their swing over neighbours and streets, material laydown and storage, hoists, site offices, welfare facilities, wash-out areas, pedestrian protection and how all of it changes as the building rises. On a tight urban lot it is often the most important document in the first year, because it decides the production rate. A site with one gate and no laydown can only work as fast as trucks arrive one at a time.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example. A hypothetical tight site can receive one concrete truck at a time at the only gate. Each truck takes 20 minutes to enter, pump and leave. A floor needs 200 cubic metres of concrete; at 8 cubic metres a truck, that is 25 trucks, about 8 hours and 20 minutes of pouring. If the street permit allows only 7 hours of deliveries a day, the pour cannot finish in one day, which forces a construction joint and a second pour. A second gate, or a street occupancy permit for a pump on the street, turns that into one day. The logistics plan is where you find that out, before the floor cycle is promised.

Earth, water and temporary works

Earthworks are the cutting, filling, moving and compacting of soil. The key numbers are volumes, how much the soil swells when dug and shrinks when compacted, where the surplus goes, and what it costs to haul and dispose of. Contaminated soil changes the cost by an order of magnitude, so environmental testing comes before the earthworks price is relied on.

Dewatering lowers or controls the groundwater so the excavation stays dry and stable. It can be as simple as pumps in a sump or as complex as a ring of wells. Pumping water out of the ground can draw down the water table under neighbouring buildings and cause them to settle, and the discharged water usually needs a permit and treatment.

Temporary works are the structures that exist only during construction: excavation support such as soldier piles and lagging, sheet piles, struts and anchors; formwork and shoring; scaffolds; crane bases. They are structures in every sense, designed for loads, and they fail like structures. The fact that they are removed later does not make them less dangerous now.

How the best do it

The strongest contractors treat temporary works with the same rigour as permanent works. A common practice on major projects is to appoint a temporary works coordinator: a named, competent person who keeps a register of every temporary structure, makes sure each has a designer and a design check, and gives a written permit to load before anything is stressed or a hole is dug past its design depth. Deep excavations are also fitted with instruments, such as inclinometers that measure wall movement and piezometers that measure water pressure, with trigger levels set in advance. A small developer can copy this: require a temporary works register and a named coordinator in the contract, and ask for the monitoring readings weekly.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: site preparation, demolition and remediation costs can be treated differently from building costs for tax purposes; ask your tax adviser how they are classified. Liability: excavation can damage neighbours, so check your insurance, the contractor's insurance and any party-wall or support obligations. Banking: lenders often release little money for site work until permits and the geotechnical report are in hand. Governance: name who may approve a change to excavation depth or support. Estate: environmental and survey records stay with the land and its owners. Exit: a buyer will ask for the final survey, the compaction records and any remediation sign-off.

Professional sign-off required: licensed land surveyor, for control and set-out; geotechnical engineer, for earthworks and dewatering criteria; licensed professional engineer, for the design of excavation support and other temporary works.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating ground and water as known when they are only sampled. Boreholes describe a few points; the site is everything between them. The control is to price site work with measured unit rates rather than a lump sum where the quantity is uncertain, carry a ground contingency, and require monitoring with trigger levels that stop the work if the ground behaves differently from the design.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner accepts a single lump-sum price for earthworks and dewatering on an uninvestigated site, believing the risk has moved to the contractor. It has not. It will come back as a claim for differing site conditions, a dispute over what was foreseeable, or a contractor who walks away.

Callback

In Week 31, Pax and Cole taught desk due diligence: environmental and geotechnical screening before you buy. Site work is where that diligence is tested. Every gap in the desk study becomes a site question with a price attached, and it is cheapest to answer before mobilisation.

Recap

Site work has six systems: survey control, logistics, earthworks, dewatering, temporary works and utilities. Keep one survey truth and protect it. Plan logistics as the production limit. Treat temporary works as real structures with a designer, a check, a register and monitoring. Price uncertain quantities by unit rate and watch the ground with trigger levels.

Next: Ford on Failure Forensics: the Nicoll Highway excavation collapse in Singapore, 2004.
checklist: I have one survey control network, reconciled to one datum, and the surveyor protects and checks it.
I require surveyor certification of foundations, column lines and floor levels before they are covered.
I have reviewed the site logistics plan as the production limit for the first year.
I have environmental testing before I rely on any earthworks price.
I require a temporary works register and a named temporary works coordinator.
I know the trigger levels for excavation and groundwater monitoring and who acts on them.
I price uncertain quantities by unit rate and carry a ground contingency.
head: Field checklist
speak: Site work is the first irreversible spend. It has six systems: survey control, the logistics plan, earthworks, dewatering, temporary works and utilities. Survey control means one network of benchmarks on one datum, protected and checked, because a datum error can put the ground floor below the flood level. The logistics plan is the production limit on a tight site: one gate and one truck at a time can turn a one-day pour into two. Earthworks depend on volumes, swell, shrinkage and disposal, and contamination changes everything. Dewatering keeps the hole dry but can settle the neighbours. Temporary works are real structures that fail like real structures, so each needs a designer, a check, a register and monitoring with trigger levels. The ground is only sampled, so I price uncertain quantities by unit rate, carry a ground contingency, and make sure someone has the authority to stop work when the readings say so.
terms: Survey control — the fixed reference points and elevations from which every part of a building is set out.
Dewatering — lowering or controlling groundwater so an excavation stays dry and stable.
Temporary works — structures that exist only during construction, such as excavation support, shoring and scaffolds.

hostile.q: You have a lump-sum earthworks price from a reputable contractor. Why are you carrying a ground contingency as well?
hostile.a: Because the lump sum covers what the contractor priced, which is the ground described in our report. If the ground differs, the contract allows a claim for differing site conditions, and if the contractor's losses are large enough, we may face a dispute or a default. The contingency is sized from the gaps in the investigation, and the monitoring gives us early warning before the cost grows.

title: Nicoll Highway 2004: When the Temporary Wall Was the Real Structure
summary: In April 2004, a deep excavation for a new rail line in Singapore collapsed beside the Nicoll Highway, killing four workers and bringing down part of the road. An official inquiry found errors in the design of the temporary support and readings of excessive wall movement that did not lead to decisive action. Ford takes it through seven steps.
body:
The Nicoll Highway collapse is the clearest modern lesson that temporary works are structures, that instruments are only useful if someone acts on them, and that a design error can hide in one connection until the day the ground finds it.

Recall

Q. What is a temporary works coordinator?

A. A named, competent person who keeps a register of every temporary structure, makes sure each has a designer and a check, and permits it to be loaded only when it is ready.

Q. What is a design-to-cost target?

A. The cost ceiling given to each design discipline, derived from the value the building must achieve.

Q. What is an accessible route?

A. A continuous, unobstructed path that a person using a wheelchair can travel, connecting accessible elements and spaces in and around a building, as defined by the adopted accessibility standard.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, your projects will dig holes, sometimes deep ones, beside streets and neighbours. The temporary wall that holds the ground back while the basement is built will be designed by someone you never meet, under a contract you sign. This case shows what goes wrong in that hidden layer. The broad facts are from the official inquiry; read its report for the engineering detail before you quote specifics.

Step 1: Timeline

Singapore was building a new underground rail line, later called the Circle Line. Near the Nicoll Highway, the contractor was excavating a deep cut-and-cover tunnel section, held open by retaining walls braced with levels of horizontal steel struts. On 20 April 2004, as excavation reached the lower levels, the support system failed, the excavation collapsed, and part of the Nicoll Highway above fell into it. Four workers died. The government appointed a committee of inquiry, which reported the following year, and the affected section of the line was realigned.

Step 2: Key decisions

The inquiry identified two groups of decisions. The first was in design. The temporary retaining system was analysed with a method that, the inquiry found, overstated the strength of the soft marine clay, so the wall deflections and the loads in the struts were underestimated. A key connection in the strut system was also found to be under-designed. The second group was in construction management: instrument readings showed the walls moving more than predicted as the excavation deepened, and the work continued without decisive action to stop, review and strengthen.

Step 3: Assumptions

The designers assumed the soil model was adequate for soft clay. The site team assumed that readings above the expected range could be managed by back-analysis and revised predictions rather than by stopping. Everyone assumed that a temporary system, because it was temporary, carried less consequence than the permanent tunnel. In fact it was holding back the ground beneath a major road.

Step 4: Incentives

A large rail project carries heavy schedule pressure and heavy costs of delay. Stopping an excavation to re-analyse and strengthen is expensive and visible. Continuing feels productive. When the people reading the instruments also carry the schedule, the incentive is to interpret the readings, not to act on them. That is not a criticism of individuals; it is a structural feature of who holds which decision.

Say that out loud now.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The instrumentation did its job: it recorded movement beyond expectations, over weeks. The warning signs were in the data. What was missing was a firm link between the readings and an action. Trigger levels that are revised upward each time they are exceeded stop being triggers. In the final period, visible distress in the strut system also appeared.

Step 6: Point of no return

The physical point of no return came when the under-designed connections began to fail and the load shifted to members that could not carry it, a progressive failure that ran through the bracing in a short time. The decision point of no return was earlier: the last moment when stopping excavation and adding support would have held the wall. After that moment, the ground decided.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause was a temporary works system designed with an unconservative soil model and a weak connection, combined with a monitoring regime whose trigger levels did not force an independent stop-and-review. Either defect alone might have been caught. Together they were fatal.

What it means at small scale

Translate it to a hypothetical urban building with one basement level beside a busy street. The contractor's shoring designer specifies soldier piles with timber lagging and one row of tiebacks. The monitoring plan sets a horizontal movement trigger of, say, 15 millimetres at the top of the wall, with an alert level of 10. At 12 millimetres, the superintendent wants to keep digging to finish before a holiday. The owner's question at that moment is the whole lesson: "Who designed the shoring, who checked it, and what does the designer say we do at this reading?" If the answer is that nobody independent checked it, and the plan says only to "review", you have the conditions of 2004 in miniature.

Now the money. Stopping for a week to add a second row of anchors might cost a hypothetical 150,000 dollars of work and delay. A shoring failure beside a street can cost the neighbour's building, the street, the utilities beneath it and a criminal investigation. There is no sensible comparison.

The prevention rule

Rule 109: Never let temporary works that hold back ground or water be loaded until they have a named designer, an independent design check and a monitoring plan whose trigger levels stop the work automatically, with the stop decision held by someone who does not own the schedule.

Professional sign-off required: licensed professional engineer, for the design of excavation support; geotechnical engineer, for the soil parameters and the monitoring triggers; an independent checking engineer, for the temporary works design on any deep excavation.

Three questions for any deep excavation

You will not read a shoring design calculation line by line, and you should not try. What you can do is ask three questions that would have changed the outcome in 2004. First: what soil model and parameters did the designer use, and did the geotechnical engineer agree with them in writing? Second: who checked the design, and were they independent of the designer and the contractor? Third: what is the stop level on each instrument, who can call the stop, and what happens in the hour after it is called?

If any answer is vague, the excavation is not ready. If the answers are clear but the readings later approach the action level, ask a fourth question before the next lift of excavation: has the designer re-run the analysis with the measured movement, and does the revised prediction still sit inside the stop level? An excavation is a structure being built downward, and every lift is a new load case.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is monitoring that records everything and controls nothing. The control is a written trigger action plan: green, amber and red levels for each instrument, a named action for each, and a rule that a red level stops excavation until the designer and checker have signed a revised design.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks the shoring is the contractor's problem because it is temporary and it is in the contractor's scope. It is in their scope. It is on your land, beside your neighbours, under your name.

Callback

In Week 99, Champlain Towers South taught that a structural warning is a safety decision first. In Week 108, Sampoong taught that changes must be re-checked as a whole. Nicoll Highway adds the instrument: a warning written by a machine is still a warning, and it needs an owner with authority to stop.

Recap

In 2004 a deep excavation in Singapore collapsed after a temporary support system designed with an unconservative soil model and a weak connection was loaded beyond its capacity, while readings of excessive movement did not trigger a stop. Rule 109 requires a designer, an independent check and triggers that stop the work.

Next: Priya on The Money: what site work costs, where its cost is uncertain, and how lenders treat it.
checklist: I know who designed and who independently checked every temporary works item that holds back ground or water.
I have a written trigger action plan with green, amber and red levels for each instrument.
A red trigger level stops excavation until the designer and checker sign a revised design.
The stop decision sits with someone who does not own the schedule.
I receive monitoring readings weekly and read them against the triggers.
I never allow trigger levels to be raised without a signed design review.
head: Field checklist
speak: On 20 April 2004, a deep excavation for Singapore's new rail line collapsed beside the Nicoll Highway, killing four workers and bringing down part of the road. The official inquiry found two kinds of failure. In design, the temporary retaining system used a soil model that overstated the strength of soft clay, and a key strut connection was under-designed. In management, instruments showed the walls moving more than predicted, and work continued without a decisive stop. Temporary works are real structures, and instruments only help if someone acts on them. So my rule is Rule 109: no temporary works that hold back ground or water are loaded until they have a named designer, an independent check, and a monitoring plan whose trigger levels stop the work automatically, with the stop decision held by someone who does not own the schedule.
terms: Cut-and-cover — building an underground structure by excavating from the surface, building it, and backfilling over it.
Strut — a horizontal compression member that braces the walls of an excavation against each other.
Trigger action plan — a set of preset instrument levels, each tied to a required action, ending with a stop.

hostile.q: The shoring is in the contractor's scope and they carry the insurance. Why are you, the owner, paying for an independent checker?
hostile.a: Because if the shoring fails, the street, the neighbour's building and the people beside the hole do not care whose scope it was. The loss lands on the project, the claim lands on me as owner, and the insurance may not cover all of it. An independent check of a deep excavation costs little against that. I also want the monitoring triggers to stop the work automatically, so the decision does not depend on someone under schedule pressure.

rule: Rule 109: Never let temporary works that hold back ground or water be loaded until they have a named designer, an independent design check and a monitoring plan whose trigger levels stop the work automatically, with the stop decision held by someone who does not own the schedule.

title: Site Work Money: Small Share of Cost, Large Share of Surprise
summary: Site work is usually a modest slice of hard cost but carries much of the early uncertainty: rock, soft ground, water, contamination and buried utilities. This lesson shows how that uncertainty moves cost, schedule, interest and the lender's draw schedule, and how to price it. Warrick's Wealth Ledger closes it.
body:
The money in site work is not in the average cost, which is small. It is in the spread of outcomes, which is wide, and in the fact that it lands at the start of the project, when every day of delay is paid for in interest on land and early costs.

Recall

Q. What does Rule 109 require before temporary works are loaded?

A. A named designer, an independent design check and a monitoring plan whose trigger levels stop the work automatically, with the stop held by someone who does not own the schedule.

Q. In the reverse-engineered design budget, which two inputs moved the hard-cost budget most?

A. The investors' required yield on cost and the net operating income.

Q. What is the difference between an elevator's capacity and its handling capacity?

A. Rated capacity is the load a car may carry; handling capacity is how many people the elevator system can move in a period, which sets wait times and depends on the number, speed and size of cars.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, lenders are usually least willing to fund the earliest part of a project, and site work is the earliest physical work. If site work overruns, you are paying for it largely with equity, at the most expensive moment, while interest runs on the land loan. Understanding the shape of that risk is how you size contingency and negotiate the loan.

Where site work cost is uncertain

Five drivers carry most of the spread. Ground: rock is slow and costly to excavate, while soft ground may need improvement or heavier support. Water: dewatering systems can run for months, with energy, monitoring and discharge permits. Contamination: soil that cannot be reused or dumped as clean fill must be tested, segregated, transported and disposed of at licensed facilities, at a far higher cost per tonne. Utilities: unrecorded or mislocated pipes and cables cause stoppages, redesigns and damages. Neighbours: underpinning, monitoring, condition surveys and claims.

Worked example: pricing contaminated soil

A hypothetical site has 10,000 cubic metres of excavation for a basement. In the base case, all of it is clean fill, hauled off at a hypothetical 25 dollars per cubic metre including loading and tipping: 250,000 dollars.

The environmental desk study flags a former fuel station on the corner. Testing suggests 15 percent of the soil, 1,500 cubic metres, may be contaminated. Contaminated soil might cost, say, 150 dollars per cubic metre to test, segregate, transport and dispose of. Now the cost is 8,500 times 25, which is 212,500 dollars, plus 1,500 times 150, which is 225,000 dollars, a total of 437,500 dollars. That is 75 percent more than the base case, from a fraction of the volume.

And if the contamination is 30 percent rather than 15, the cost becomes 7,000 times 25 plus 3,000 times 150, which is 175,000 plus 450,000, or 625,000 dollars. The swing between 15 and 30 percent is 187,500 dollars. That is why you test before you price, and why you price disposal by unit rate per tonne or cubic metre, with a defined measurement method, rather than as a lump sum.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example: what a delay costs at the start

Now the time dimension. Suppose dewatering fails and the excavation floods, adding six weeks. The project has spent a hypothetical 12,000,000 dollars so far on land and early costs, financed by a land loan of 7,000,000 dollars at a hypothetical 8 percent and equity of 5,000,000 dollars.

Interest on the land loan for six weeks is 7,000,000 times 0.08 times 6 over 52, about 64,600 dollars. Add the contractor's time-related costs, say site establishment, supervision and plant at 25,000 dollars a week, another 150,000 dollars. Add the cost of the delay to completion at the far end, where the construction loan will be much larger. If the full construction loan peaks at 30,000,000 dollars drawn, six extra weeks of interest near the end could cost another 30,000,000 times 0.08 times 6 over 52, about 277,000 dollars, plus six weeks of lost rent. The flood costs perhaps 500,000 dollars, most of it not at the flood.

How lenders treat site work

Lenders typically want the geotechnical report, environmental reports, a permit and a fixed or capped construction price before they commit to fund construction. Many structure the loan so that the borrower's equity is spent first, which means early overruns fall on equity. Some will fund site work as part of the construction loan once conditions precedent are met; others will not until the building permit is issued. The terms are commercial practice and negotiable. What is not negotiable is the in-balance test: if your cost to complete rises above the money available, you fund the gap.

A practical tactic is to carry a separate site and ground contingency in the budget, visible to the lender, sized from the specific uncertainties above rather than as a flat percentage. A contingency with a reason behind each line is easier to defend and less likely to be raided for other costs.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet: because equity goes in first, the early months of a project are when your own cash is most exposed and least protected by the lender's money. Keep your personal liquidity floor intact through site work, and do not commit equity to a second project until the first has its foundations in and its ground risk largely retired.

Who carries the ground risk

The contract decides who pays first for ground that differs from the report. Many standard forms include a differing site conditions clause, under which the contractor is paid for conditions materially different from those indicated in the contract documents or ordinarily encountered. That clause is commercial practice, not a law, and its wording varies. With it, the owner carries the risk of the unknown but gets lower bids, because contractors do not price a gamble. Without it, contractors price the gamble and still claim when it goes wrong. Most experienced owners keep the clause, invest in a better site investigation, and attach a geotechnical baseline that defines what was expected.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a site budget built on clean-ground assumptions, priced as a lump sum, with no contingency tied to the known uncertainties. The control is to test early, price the uncertain items by unit rate with a measurement method, and carry a named ground contingency that the lender can see.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner counts only the direct cost of a site problem and forgets that a delay at the start pushes the whole schedule, and that the interest at the end, on a larger loan, is the bigger bill.

Time and energy, a monthly thread

Site work is also where your own time gets eaten. Early-morning pours, utility shutdowns and inspections cluster at the start of the job, often against a rotating shift pattern. Decide in advance which site events need you in person, usually the first excavation past design depth, the first concrete pour and any red trigger, and delegate the rest to your project manager with a written threshold for when to call you.

Protect the sleep around those events. A decision made at the end of a long night shift is a weaker decision, and site work is full of decisions that cannot be undone.

Callback

In Week 40, Priya taught the draw and the in-balance test. Site work is where the test first bites: an early overrun, before most of the loan is drawn, comes straight from equity, and it shrinks the cushion you have for everything that follows.

Recap

Site work cost is uncertain through ground, water, contamination, utilities and neighbours. Test before pricing, use unit rates for uncertain quantities, and size a named ground contingency. Count the interest and time cost of delay, which is often larger than the direct cost, and remember that early overruns fall on equity.

Next: REGA on The Rules: excavation safety, utility locates, stormwater and discharge permits, and how Canada and Guyana approach them.
checklist: I have environmental and geotechnical testing before I rely on site work prices.
I price contaminated soil, rock and dewatering by unit rate with a measurement method.
I carry a named ground contingency sized from specific uncertainties.
I calculate the interest and time cost of a site delay at both ends of the schedule.
I know when my lender will fund site work and what conditions apply.
I keep my personal liquidity floor intact through site work.
head: Field checklist
speak: Site work is a small share of hard cost but a large share of the surprise. The spread comes from ground, water, contamination, utilities and neighbours. In my example, 10,000 cubic metres of clean soil costs 250,000 dollars to haul away. If 15 percent is contaminated and costs 150 dollars a cubic metre instead of 25, the total becomes 437,500 dollars, and at 30 percent it is 625,000. So I test before I price, and I price uncertain items by unit rate. Delay matters too: six weeks of flooding costs interest on the land loan now, the contractor's time costs, and interest on a much larger loan at the end, plus lost rent. Lenders usually want equity spent first, so early overruns land on my equity. I carry a named ground contingency the lender can see, and I keep my personal liquidity floor intact until the ground risk is retired.
terms: Unit rate — a price per measured unit of work, such as dollars per cubic metre, used where the quantity is uncertain.
Ground contingency — a budget reserve sized specifically for uncertainties in ground, water and contamination.
Equity first — a loan structure in which the borrower's equity is spent before the lender advances funds.

hostile.q: Your ground contingency is 600,000 dollars on a 1,500,000-dollar site package. Isn't that padding?
hostile.a: No. Every line has a reason. 187,500 dollars covers the swing from 15 to 30 percent contaminated soil found in testing. The rest covers dewatering running longer than planned, rock in the two borings that hit it, and unrecorded utilities on the street frontage. If those risks do not happen, the money is released. If they do, I would rather it sat in a visible line than came out of equity mid-dig.

title: The Rules Under the Ground: Excavation Safety, Locates, Stormwater and Discharge
summary: Site work is governed by a dense web of rules: occupational safety for excavations, utility locate requirements, stormwater and erosion control, groundwater discharge permits, and duties to neighbours. This lesson explains how they work in the United States, with a Two Systems comparison of how Canada and Guyana approach the same points.
body:
Site work is where several regulators meet in one hole: the safety regulator cares about the workers, the utility cares about its pipes, the environmental regulator cares about the water you discharge, and the city cares about the street and the neighbours. Each has its own permit and its own stop-work power.

Recall

Q. Why does contaminated soil change the site budget so much?

A. Because it must be tested, segregated, transported and disposed of at licensed facilities at a much higher unit cost, so a small share of volume can dominate the cost.

Q. What is the code's alternative method provision for?

A. It lets the building official approve a design or material not described in the prescriptive code if it is shown to be at least equivalent in safety and performance.

Q. What is a fire pump for?

A. It raises water pressure for sprinklers and standpipes when the water supply alone cannot deliver the flow and pressure the system needs.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a site work violation does not just carry a fine. It can stop the job, trigger an investigation, and in a fatality bring criminal exposure. The rules are mostly enforced against the employer doing the work, but as owner you choose the contractor, set the schedule and pay for the safety measures. You need to know the main rules well enough to ask the right questions and to fund what they require.

Excavation safety

In the United States, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) sets construction safety rules in Title 29 of the Code of Federal Regulations, Part 1926. Excavations are covered in Subpart P. In broad terms, the standard requires a competent person to inspect excavations daily and after events such as rain; protective systems such as sloping, benching, shoring or shields for excavations at or above a set depth unless the excavation is in stable rock; safe access and egress; keeping spoil and equipment back from the edge; and protective systems for deeper excavations to be designed by a registered professional engineer [unverified — confirm independently the depth thresholds and exact requirements in the current regulation]. States with their own approved plans may add requirements.

The key term is competent person: someone who can identify existing and predictable hazards and has authority to take prompt corrective action. Notice the second half. A person without authority to stop the work is not, in this sense, competent. That links directly to Rule 109.

Worked example. A hypothetical trench for a sewer connection is 2 metres deep in clay beside the street. The crew wants to dig, lay the pipe and backfill in one afternoon without a trench box, because the box would take two hours to bring and set. A trench collapse at that depth can kill. The cost of the box and the two hours is perhaps a hypothetical 1,500 dollars. The rule is not a cost question; it is a condition of doing the work at all.

Utility locates

Before digging, contractors in the United States generally must notify a one-call centre, often reached by dialling 811, which notifies member utilities to mark their buried lines. The marks show approximate locations within a tolerance zone, inside which hand digging or careful methods are expected. State laws set the notice period, the marking duties and the liability for damage [unverified — confirm independently for your state]. Not every line is a member utility; private services on the site itself may not be marked, which is why a private locate survey and potholing, exposing lines by careful digging, are common practice.

Say that out loud now.

Stormwater and erosion control

Disturbing land exposes soil to rain. Under the federal Clean Water Act, construction sites disturbing at least a set area generally need coverage under a National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) stormwater permit, issued by the Environmental Protection Agency or an authorised state, and must prepare a stormwater pollution prevention plan, or SWPPP, describing erosion and sediment controls, inspections and records [unverified — confirm independently the area threshold and permit in your state]. The controls are physical: silt fences, inlet protection, stabilised construction entrances, sediment basins and covering stockpiles. The records matter as much as the fences, because inspectors check both.

Groundwater discharge and neighbours

Water pumped from an excavation is not clean just because it came from the ground. It can carry sediment and, near contaminated sites, chemicals. Discharging it to a storm drain, sewer or watercourse usually needs permission from the city, the sewer authority or the environmental regulator, and may need settlement tanks or treatment.

Neighbours have rights too. Many jurisdictions recognise a duty to provide lateral support to adjoining land, and city codes often require notice to adjoining owners before excavation near their foundations. A pre-construction condition survey of neighbouring buildings, with photographs and crack measurements, is the record that separates damage you caused from damage that was already there.

Two Systems

Here is a conceptual comparison of how Canada and Guyana approach these points. Verify against primary source before relying on any of it.

In Canada, workplace safety on most construction sites falls under provincial and territorial occupational health and safety legislation, not a single national code, so excavation rules, competent-person definitions and engineering requirements vary by province. Many provinces operate one-call or similar locate services, and some require locates by law. Environmental approvals for dewatering discharge and sediment control are generally provincial and municipal. The practical lesson is that the rule depends on where the site is, and the province's own regulation is the primary source.

In Guyana, occupational safety and health is governed by national legislation administered through the ministry responsible for labour, with requirements on employers for safe systems of work. Utility coordination tends to run through each utility directly rather than a single locate service, so direct requests, existing records and careful exposure of services matter more. Environmental matters, including discharges, are overseen by a national environmental agency. Expect fewer detailed prescriptive excavation rules and more reliance on the employer's general duty and on good engineering practice.

The common thread in both: the employer carries the duty, the owner shapes the conditions, and good practice from American standards is a sensible benchmark even where it is not the law.

Professional sign-off required: licensed professional engineer, for excavation protective systems where required; environmental consultant or engineer, for the stormwater plan and discharge approvals; a lawyer in the jurisdiction, for neighbour notice and support obligations.

One more practical point on records. Keep the competent person's daily excavation inspections, the stormwater inspection logs, the locate tickets and the discharge approvals in the project file, not only the contractor's. If an inspector or a neighbour's lawyer asks, the record you can produce that day is the one that counts.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming that because the contractor holds the safety duty, the owner carries none. The control is to require in the contract a site-specific safety plan, a named competent person for excavations, the stormwater plan and its records, and evidence of locates and discharge approvals before digging, and to check them.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner relies on the one-call marks alone. Marks cover member utilities within a tolerance; private lines and old abandoned services are often unmarked. Pay for a private locate and pothole before mechanical digging near any suspected service.

Callback

In Week 53, Duke taught OSHA's Focus Four hazards and the multi-employer doctrine, under which a controlling employer can be cited for hazards it could have prevented. Excavation is where that doctrine bites hardest, because one trench can expose several contractors' workers at once.

Recap

Excavations need a competent person with authority, protective systems and engineered design at depth. Locate utilities through one-call and private surveys, and pothole. Stormwater needs a permit, a plan, controls and records. Discharges need approval, and neighbours need notice and a condition survey. Canada sets most of this provincially; Guyana relies on national safety and environmental bodies and direct utility coordination.

Next: Quincy on The Numbers: an earthworks calculation from cut and fill to trucks and cost.
checklist: I require a site-specific safety plan and a named competent person for excavations.
I see evidence of one-call locates, a private locate survey and potholing before mechanical digging.
I have stormwater permit coverage, a pollution prevention plan and inspection records where required.
I have approval for any groundwater discharge and know where the water goes.
I have notified adjoining owners where required and completed a pre-construction condition survey.
I know which regulator and which regulation applies where the site is.
head: Field checklist
speak: Site work sits under several regulators at once. For safety, OSHA's excavation standard in Part 1926, Subpart P, requires a competent person with authority to act, protective systems such as sloping, shoring or shields at depth, and engineered design for deeper excavations, but I confirm the thresholds in the current regulation. For utilities, contractors notify the one-call centre, often 811, but private lines may not be marked, so I pay for a private locate and potholing. Stormwater generally needs permit coverage, a pollution prevention plan, physical controls and records. Pumped groundwater needs approval before discharge. Neighbours need notice and a condition survey. In Canada most of this is provincial; in Guyana, national safety and environmental bodies and direct utility coordination matter more. The employer holds the safety duty, but I set the conditions, so I require the plans and evidence in the contract and I check them before digging.
terms: Competent person — someone able to identify hazards on site who also has authority to take prompt corrective action.
One-call centre — a service, often reached by dialling 811 in the United States, that notifies utilities to mark buried lines before digging.
Stormwater pollution prevention plan (SWPPP) — a site plan describing erosion and sediment controls, inspections and records required under a stormwater permit.

hostile.q: The utility marked the street. Why did your contractor stop to pothole, and why are you paying for a private locate survey?
hostile.a: Because the marks cover member utilities only, within a tolerance zone, and our site has old private services from the previous building. Striking a live line can injure a worker, shut a neighbour's service and stop the job for weeks. The private locate and potholing cost a day and a few thousand dollars. The marks are where the duty starts, not where it ends.

title: Earthworks by the Numbers: From Cut and Fill to Trucks and Dollars
summary: A worked earthworks calculation, step by step with units: excavation volume, swell to loose volume, shrinkage of fill, the earthworks balance, truckloads, haul days and cost. Hypothetical round numbers throughout, and a check on how a small change in assumptions moves the answer.
body:
Earthworks cost is volume multiplied by the right factor, multiplied by the right rate. Most errors come from using the wrong volume: bank, loose or compacted.

Recall

Q. What is a competent person under excavation safety rules?

A. Someone who can identify existing and predictable hazards and has authority to take prompt corrective action.

Q. What is a facade-to-floor ratio?

A. External wall area divided by floor area, a driver of envelope cost.

Q. What does compartmentation do in a fire strategy?

A. It divides a building into fire-resisting compartments so a fire is held in one area long enough for people to escape and firefighters to act.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, earthworks prices come to you as unit rates per cubic metre and as lump sums. If you do not know which volume a rate refers to, you cannot check the quantity, compare bids or measure the work for payment. This lesson walks through the arithmetic once, so you can audit it on any site.

Three volumes of the same soil

Soil has three volumes. Bank volume is the soil in place, undisturbed, as it sits in the ground. Loose volume is the same soil after digging, larger because air gets in; the increase is called swell. Compacted volume is the soil after it is placed and compacted as fill, usually smaller than bank volume; the decrease is called shrinkage. Typical swell and shrinkage factors depend on the soil type and should come from the geotechnical engineer, not from a textbook.

Step 1: The excavation in bank volume

A hypothetical basement excavation is 40 metres long, 30 metres wide and 4 metres deep, with the sides supported vertically by shoring.

Bank volume equals 40 times 30 times 4, which is 4,800 cubic metres.

Add an allowance for the working space and footing excavations below the main floor: say 200 cubic metres. Total bank volume to excavate: 5,000 cubic metres.

Step 2: Convert to loose volume for hauling

The geotechnical report describes stiff clay with an assumed swell of 30 percent. Loose volume equals bank volume times 1.30.

5,000 times 1.30 equals 6,500 loose cubic metres.

Trucks carry loose soil, so truck counts must use this number.

Say that out loud now.

Step 3: The earthworks balance

The site needs fill elsewhere: behind the basement walls and under the ground-floor slab outside the building, a compacted volume of 1,200 cubic metres. But the clay is not suitable as structural fill; the geotechnical engineer specifies imported granular fill. So none of the excavated clay can be reused, and the site is in surplus.

All 6,500 loose cubic metres must leave the site.

The imported fill must be bought in. For the granular fill, the supplier sells by loose volume, and the geotechnical engineer gives a factor of 1.25 loose cubic metres for each compacted cubic metre.

1,200 times 1.25 equals 1,500 loose cubic metres to import.

Step 4: Trucks and days

A truck carries 10 loose cubic metres. Export loads: 6,500 divided by 10 equals 650 truckloads. Import loads: 1,500 divided by 10 equals 150 loads.

The logistics plan allows one truck every 10 minutes at the gate, over a 7-hour permitted working day: 42 trucks a day. Export takes 650 divided by 42, about 15.5 days, if the excavator keeps pace. Excavating 5,000 bank cubic metres at an assumed 400 bank cubic metres a day takes 12.5 days, so the gate, not the machine, is the bottleneck. Plan for about 16 working days of export.

Step 5: Cost

Hypothetical rates, all including labour, plant and margin:

  • Excavation and loading: 8 dollars per bank cubic metre. 5,000 times 8 equals 40,000 dollars.
  • Haul and tipping of clean clay: 18 dollars per loose cubic metre. 6,500 times 18 equals 117,000 dollars.
  • Imported granular fill, delivered: 35 dollars per loose cubic metre. 1,500 times 35 equals 52,500 dollars.
  • Placing and compacting fill: 12 dollars per compacted cubic metre. 1,200 times 12 equals 14,400 dollars.
  • Compaction testing: an allowance of 6,000 dollars.

Total: 40,000 plus 117,000 plus 52,500 plus 14,400 plus 6,000 equals 229,900 dollars, about 230,000 dollars.

Step 6: The common error, checked

Second worked example. Suppose a bid priced haul at 18 dollars per cubic metre but applied it to the bank volume of 5,000 rather than the loose 6,500. The bid shows 90,000 dollars for haul instead of 117,000. It looks 27,000 dollars cheaper. When the trucks are counted on site, the contractor will claim the difference, or argue the rate was per loose cubic metre all along. Your contract must state, for every earthworks rate, which volume it applies to and how it is measured: by survey of the excavation before and after, by truck tickets, or by weighbridge tonnes.

Now sensitivity. If the swell is 40 percent rather than 30, loose volume becomes 7,000 cubic metres: 50 more truckloads, about 1.2 more days at the gate, and 9,000 dollars more haul. Small. But if 10 percent of the excavation turns out to be contaminated and costs 150 dollars per loose cubic metre instead of 18, that is 650 loose cubic metres times 132 dollars of extra cost, about 85,800 dollars, a 37 percent increase on the whole package. The volume factors matter; contamination matters far more.

Step 7: Read it back as a lender would

A lender's monitor does not need the arithmetic; it needs the logic and the risk. Say it in four sentences. "The basement is 5,000 bank cubic metres of clay. With 30 percent swell that is 6,500 loose cubic metres, 650 trucks, about 16 working days because the gate allows 42 trucks a day. None of the clay is reusable, so we import 1,500 loose cubic metres of granular fill. The package is about 230,000 dollars, priced by unit rate on stated volumes, with contamination as the main risk and a contingency held against it."

That last clause matters. If the monitor knows contamination is the main risk, a later claim for contaminated soil looks like a risk you identified, not a surprise you missed. Name the risk in the first report, and you will be believed in the next one.

Step 8: Measure what was really done

At the end, compare the survey of the finished excavation with the original ground survey to get the true bank volume removed. Compare that with the truck tickets divided by the swell factor. If 680 loads were tipped against an expected 650, either the swell was higher, the excavation was larger, or some loads were part-full. The reconciliation tells you which, and it is the evidence for the final payment.

Keep the reconciliation on one page with the original estimate beside it. Over a few projects, that page becomes your own record of real swell factors, real gate rates and real contamination shares, which is better data than any textbook figure.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an earthworks contract that does not say which volume each rate applies to or how it is measured. The control is a measurement clause naming bank, loose or compacted volume for every rate, the method of measurement, and who surveys the excavation before and after.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner assumes excavated soil can be reused as fill to balance the site. Only soil the geotechnical engineer approves as suitable can be reused. Clay, organic soil and contaminated soil usually cannot.

Callback

In Week 49, Marco and Quincy taught the schedule of values and cost codes. Earthworks show why a clear unit of measure belongs in every line. A rate without a stated unit and measurement method is not a price; it is an argument waiting for the first truck count.

Recap

Bank volume becomes loose volume by swell and compacted volume by shrinkage. Haul uses loose volume. Balance cut against fill only with suitable soil. Count trucks and gate capacity to get days. Price each item on its stated volume and test how swell and contamination move the total.

Next: Duke on The Room: the pre-excavation meeting where the schedule meets the shoring.
checklist: I know whether each earthworks rate applies to bank, loose or compacted volume.
I use swell and shrinkage factors from the geotechnical engineer, not a textbook.
I reuse excavated soil as fill only where the geotechnical engineer approves it.
I check truck counts against gate capacity in the logistics plan.
My contract states the measurement method for earthworks: survey, truck tickets or weighbridge.
I test how swell and contamination change the total before I accept a price.
head: Field checklist
speak: Earthworks are volume times the right factor times the right rate. Soil has three volumes: bank, in the ground; loose, after digging, larger by the swell; and compacted, as fill, usually smaller. My example basement is 40 by 30 by 4 metres, 4,800 cubic metres, plus 200 for footings, so 5,000 bank cubic metres. At 30 percent swell that is 6,500 loose cubic metres to haul, 650 truckloads at 10 cubic metres each. The clay cannot be reused, so I import 1,500 loose cubic metres of granular fill for 1,200 compacted. At 42 trucks a day the gate, not the excavator, sets about 16 days. The total is about 230,000 dollars. The common error is pricing haul on bank volume, which hides 27,000 dollars that comes back as a claim. So every rate names its volume and its measurement method.
terms: Bank volume — the volume of soil in place, undisturbed, before excavation.
Swell — the increase in volume when soil is excavated and loosened.
Earthworks balance — the comparison of soil cut against soil needed as fill, showing whether a site has a surplus to export or a shortfall to import.

hostile.q: Your bid comparison shows Contractor B is 27,000 dollars cheaper on haul. Why are you not taking it?
hostile.a: Because Contractor B applied the haul rate to the bank volume of 5,000 cubic metres, while trucks carry loose soil, about 6,500 cubic metres with this clay's swell. The real haul quantity is 30 percent higher, so the saving is an error, not a price. I have asked both bidders to confirm their rates against loose volume with truck tickets as the measurement method, and the comparison closes up.

title: The Pre-Excavation Meeting: When the Schedule Meets the Shoring
summary: A realistic pre-excavation meeting before a deep basement dig beside a street. The contractor wants to start before the shoring check is finished, the monitoring plan has no stop level, and a neighbour's lawyer has written. Learn the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question, and when to stay silent.
body:
The pre-excavation meeting is the last calm moment before the ground starts making decisions. Use it to confirm that every temporary structure has a designer, a check and a stop level, and that the person who can stop the dig is in the room.

Recall

Q. Which volume do trucks carry when soil is hauled?

A. Loose volume, which is bank volume increased by the swell factor.

Q. What is a design freeze?

A. A point after which the design may change only through the formal change procedure.

Q. What is the difference between a smoke control system and smoke venting?

A. A smoke control system uses fans, pressure differences or airflow to manage smoke movement and protect escape routes, while venting releases smoke through openings, often relying on natural buoyancy.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, here is the room. Your project has a basement excavation 4 metres deep beside a busy street and a neighbour's older masonry building. Around the table: the contractor's project manager and superintendent, the shoring designer, the geotechnical engineer, your project manager, and you. The contractor's schedule shows excavation starting Monday. It is Thursday.

Scene one: start before the check

The project manager opens: "The shoring design is done. The independent check is due next Wednesday, but the first two metres are within the self-supporting depth, so we want to start Monday and keep the crew."

The question behind the question: will the owner trade a check for a schedule?

Say: "I understand the crew pressure, and I want to help with it. But we agreed in the contract that no excavation starts until the shoring design is checked. Let us see if the checker can finish sooner. If the first stage really is independent of the shoring, I want the shoring designer and the geotechnical engineer to say so in writing, with the depth limit marked on the drawing, before Monday."

Never say: "Two metres is nothing; just be careful." That sentence is how the competent-person duty and Rule 109 are given away in one breath.

Then stay silent and let the shoring designer answer. The designer is the person who knows whether the first stage is truly independent.

Say that out loud now.

Scene two: the plan with no stop

You turn to the monitoring plan. It lists inclinometers, settlement points on the neighbour's wall and survey targets on the street, read weekly, with a "review level" of 20 millimetres.

Say: "Thank you, this is a good set of instruments. I need three changes before we dig. First, readings at least twice a week during excavation, and daily below the first strut or anchor level. Second, three levels, not one: alert, action and stop. Third, a stop level that stops excavation automatically until the designer and the checker sign a revised design. Who will hold the authority to stop?"

The superintendent says: "That's me."

Say: "Thank you. I would like the geotechnical engineer to hold it as well, so either of you can stop the dig, and neither needs the other's permission."

The question behind that: the superintendent also owns the schedule. Two keys to the stop, one of them independent of the schedule, is the design of the control.

Scene three: the neighbour's letter

Your project manager hands you a letter from the neighbour's lawyer asking for confirmation that the excavation will not damage their building and for a copy of the shoring design.

Say: "We will respond in writing through our counsel. Before Monday I want the condition survey of their building complete, with photographs and crack measurements, and I want to offer them the monitoring readings for the points on their wall. Openness now is cheaper than argument later."

Never say: "Our engineer guarantees there will be no damage." No engineer guarantees that, and the sentence becomes an admission the day a crack appears.

A worked number to have in your head: if the dig slips a week to finish the check and the condition survey, the cost is the crew standing time and a week of land interest. Say the crew costs a hypothetical 30,000 dollars a week, and land interest is about 10,000 dollars a week: about 40,000 dollars. A neighbour's claim for structural damage to an older masonry building, with legal costs, could easily exceed that many times over. You can say the comparison aloud.

Scene four: the contractor pushes back

The project manager says, with an edge: "If you delay us a week, we will be looking for an extension of time and costs."

Say: "That is fair to raise. If the delay is caused by a requirement we added beyond the contract, put it in a notice and we will deal with it under the contract. If it is a requirement the contract already contains, the independent check, then it is not a delay we caused. Either way, we will not start without it."

Then stop. You have answered. Adding more sounds like doubt.

Closing

Read back: "No excavation until the check is signed, unless the designer and the geotechnical engineer confirm the first stage is independent, in writing, with a depth limit. Monitoring twice a week, daily below the first support level, with alert, action and stop levels. Stop authority held by the superintendent and the geotechnical engineer, each alone. Condition survey complete and readings offered to the neighbour. Counsel responds to the letter."

Holding your state

The contractor's edge in scene four is a test, not an attack. Keep your voice at the pace you opened with, lower rather than louder. You are not arguing about whether to be safe; you are confirming what the contract already says. That is a calm position, and calm is what persuades a room of site professionals.

What to watch after the meeting

The meeting sets the controls; the first week tests them. Read the first readings yourself. Walk the site on the first day of excavation, look at where the spoil is placed and whether the edge is kept clear, and check the competent person's inspection record. If you see the excavator digging below the first support level before the struts or anchors are in, ask the superintendent one question: "Is this within the permit to dig?" Then wait for the answer.

You are not supervising the work. You are confirming that the controls you paid for are working, and showing the site that the owner reads what it signs.

And send the meeting note the same day. Write the start conditions, the trigger levels, the stop holders and the neighbour actions in plain sentences, and ask every attendee to reply if anything is wrong. Silence after a clear written note is agreement; silence after a conversation is not.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is leaving the meeting with a verbal understanding that the dig can start "carefully" before the check. The control is to write the start conditions as a permit to dig, signed by the temporary works coordinator, with the depth limit and the stop authority stated on it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks raising safety conditions in front of the contractor damages the relationship. Good contractors respect an owner who funds and enforces the controls, because it protects their people and their insurance too.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught acknowledge, bridge, answer. Every reply in this meeting acknowledged the pressure, bridged to the contract or the control, and answered with a condition and a date. And from Week 109's Failure Forensics, Rule 109 is the reason behind every one of them.

Recap

Do not trade the shoring check for the schedule. Turn a monitoring plan into a trigger action plan with alert, action and stop levels. Give the stop to two people, one independent of the schedule. Survey the neighbour first and share the readings. Answer a delay threat under the contract, then stop talking.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: the week on site work, with a Red Pen drill on a logistics plan.
checklist: No excavation starts until the shoring design is independently checked, or the designer certifies an independent first stage in writing.
My monitoring plan has alert, action and stop levels with named actions.
Readings increase in frequency as excavation deepens.
Stop authority is held by two people, one independent of the schedule.
The neighbour's condition survey is complete before digging.
I answer delay threats under the contract and do not argue beyond it.
I issue a written permit to dig with depth limit and stop authority.
head: Field checklist
speak: At the pre-excavation meeting I do not trade the shoring check for the schedule. If the contractor wants to start the first stage early, the shoring designer and the geotechnical engineer must confirm in writing that it is independent of the shoring, with a depth limit on the drawing. I never say two metres is nothing. A monitoring plan with one review level is not a control, so I ask for alert, action and stop levels, readings that increase as the dig deepens, and a stop that halts excavation until the designer and checker sign a revised design. Two people hold the stop, the superintendent and the geotechnical engineer, so one of them is independent of the schedule. I complete the neighbour's condition survey and offer them the readings, and counsel answers their letter. If the contractor threatens a delay claim, I answer under the contract and stop talking.
terms: Permit to dig — a written authorisation, issued by the temporary works coordinator, that states the conditions and depth limit for excavation.
Condition survey — a dated record, with photographs and measurements, of a neighbouring building's state before work begins.
Stop level — the instrument reading at which work stops automatically until the design is reviewed.

hostile.q: You are costing us a week for a check the designer says is a formality. Why are you not trusting your own consultants?
hostile.a: I do trust them, which is why I hired an independent checker too. The contract requires the check before excavation, so this is not a new demand. If the first stage is truly independent of the shoring, the designer can say so in writing with a depth limit, and you can start Monday. If not, a week is a small price against a shoring problem beside a street and an old masonry building.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 109 Review: Survey, Logistics, Earth, Water, Temporary Works and Utilities
summary: Six questions test the week on site work: survey control, logistics, earthworks volumes, dewatering, temporary works and the rules under the ground. A Red Pen drill on a hypothetical site logistics note with planted defects follows, and a two-minute boardroom drill closes the week.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: site work builds on ground and water that are only sampled, so every temporary structure needs a designer, a check and a stop, and every uncertain quantity needs a unit rate and a contingency.

Recall

Q. In the pre-excavation meeting, who should hold the authority to stop the dig?

A. Two people, each able to act alone: the contractor's superintendent and the geotechnical engineer, so that one holder is independent of the schedule.

Q. What is the last responsible moment?

A. The latest point at which a decision can be made without closing off a better option or forcing rework.

Q. What is a dead-end corridor limit?

A. The maximum length of corridor from which there is only one direction to an exit, set by the code for each occupancy, so people are not trapped.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the site work phase is short, but its decisions are permanent and often dangerous. If you can answer these six questions aloud without notes, you can sit with a civil engineer, a contractor and a lender at the start of a job and be the person who asks the right thing. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What are the six systems of site work?

Answer: Survey control, the site logistics plan, earthworks, dewatering, temporary works and utilities.

Question 2. Why does survey control need one network on one datum?

Answer: Because every element is set out from it. Two references that differ, for example a city datum and an assumed site datum, can put a floor at the wrong level, including below the design flood elevation.

Question 3. A basement excavation is 5,000 bank cubic metres in clay with 30 percent swell. How many 10-cubic-metre truckloads?

Answer: 5,000 times 1.30 is 6,500 loose cubic metres, divided by 10 is 650 loads.

Question 4. What did the Nicoll Highway inquiry find, and what is Rule 109?

Answer: A temporary support system designed with an unconservative soil model and an under-designed connection, and instrument readings of excess movement that did not trigger a stop. Rule 109: no temporary works holding back ground or water are loaded without a named designer, an independent check and trigger levels that stop the work, held by someone who does not own the schedule.

Question 5. Why does a site delay cost more than the direct cost of fixing it?

Answer: Because it adds interest on the land loan now, the contractor's time-related costs, and interest on the much larger construction loan at the end, plus lost rent, and early overruns usually fall on equity.

Question 6. The one-call marks are on the street. Is it safe to dig?

Answer: Not yet. Marks cover member utilities within a tolerance zone; private and abandoned services may be unmarked. A private locate survey and potholing come before mechanical digging, and the trench needs a competent person and a protective system at depth.

Say that out loud now.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical site logistics note from a contractor. Find the defects before you read the answers.

Site Logistics Note, Rev 0. Excavation starts Monday. Single gate on the main street; trucks every 5 minutes, 7am to 7pm. Spoil stockpiled along the north edge of the excavation to save haul. Shoring by soldier piles and lagging, design attached, check to follow. Monitoring weekly; review if movement exceeds 25 millimetres. Pumped groundwater to the street drain. Utilities marked by 811. Crane to be positioned at the northeast corner; swing over the neighbour's roof as needed. Haul priced at 18 dollars per cubic metre.

The defects:

  1. Excavation starts before the shoring check, against Rule 109 and the contract.
  2. Trucks every 5 minutes for 12 hours may exceed the street permit and the gate's real capacity; the note gives no check against permitted hours.
  3. Spoil stockpiled at the excavation edge adds load to the shoring and breaks the keep-back requirement.
  4. Weekly monitoring with a single review level is not a trigger action plan; there is no stop level or named stop authority.
  5. Groundwater discharged to the street drain with no stated approval or sediment treatment.
  6. Utilities relying on 811 marks alone, with no private locate or potholing.
  7. Crane swing over the neighbour's roof with no mention of the neighbour's agreement or the required permission.
  8. Haul rate with no stated volume basis, bank or loose, and no measurement method.

Recap

Site work runs on six systems. Keep one survey truth. Treat logistics as the production limit. Count bank, loose and compacted volumes correctly and price uncertain items by unit rate. Treat dewatering as a risk to neighbours and a discharge to permit. Give every temporary structure a designer, an independent check and a trigger action plan with a stop held by someone independent of the schedule. Locate every utility, not only the marked ones.

Boardroom drill

Explain this week in two minutes to an investor who asks, "Why does your site budget carry so much contingency, and how do you stop the dig from going wrong?" Set a timer and speak before reading the model answer.

Model answer: "Site work is a small part of the cost and a large part of the uncertainty, because we only sample the ground. Our contingency has a reason for every line: contamination found in testing, rock in two borings, dewatering duration, and unrecorded utilities on the street. If those do not happen, the money is released. Each is priced by unit rate, so we pay for what is really there. On safety and control, every temporary structure that holds back ground or water has a named designer, an independent check and a monitoring plan with a stop level that halts excavation until the design is reviewed, and the geotechnical engineer can stop the dig without asking the contractor. We completed a condition survey of the neighbour before digging and share our readings with them. That is how a hole beside a street stays a hole and not a headline."

Scoring yourself

Count your answers. Six clear answers means you are ready for the foundation weeks. Four or five means reread the lesson for each miss today, not later. Fewer than four means rehearse the six systems and Rule 109 aloud tomorrow morning and take the questions again. For the Red Pen, write down how many of the eight defects you found before reading them. Most people miss the spoil at the edge and the haul rate's volume basis, which are the two that cost money quietly.

Then look at what you missed and ask why. Missing a safety defect usually means you were reading for cost. Missing a cost defect usually means you were reading for safety. A complete reviewer reads every line for both, in two passes if necessary.

Finally, rehearse the boardroom answer once more tomorrow without reading it. If the phrase "who can stop the work" does not come out of your mouth unprompted, you have not yet absorbed the week.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk in reviewing this week is remembering the arithmetic and forgetting the authority. Volumes and rates are easy to rehearse. The harder habit is asking, every time, who can stop the work and whether they are independent.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads the Red Pen defects and nods. Mark them yourself first, then count how many you missed, and write that number in your decision journal.

Callback

In Week 108, the design checkpoint taught that decisions lock in order. Site work is the first decision that is poured, compacted and backfilled. Rule 108 asked for a re-check before a change reaches site; Rule 109 asks for a check before the ground is opened.

head: The six questions
speak: Site work builds on ground and water that are only sampled. It has six systems: survey control, logistics, earthworks, dewatering, temporary works and utilities. I keep one survey network on one datum. I treat the logistics plan as the production limit. For earthworks I keep bank, loose and compacted volumes straight: 5,000 bank cubic metres of clay at 30 percent swell is 6,500 loose, or 650 truckloads. I price uncertain items by unit rate with a measurement method, and I carry a named ground contingency, because early overruns fall on equity and delays cost interest at both ends. Dewatering can settle neighbours and needs a discharge approval. Utilities need a private locate and potholing beyond the one-call marks. And from Nicoll Highway in 2004, Rule 109: every temporary structure holding back ground or water needs a named designer, an independent check and trigger levels that stop the work, held by someone independent of the schedule.
terms: Trigger action plan — a set of preset instrument levels, each tied to a required action, ending with a stop.
Loose volume — the volume of excavated soil after digging, used to count truckloads.
Potholing — exposing a buried utility by careful hand or vacuum digging to confirm its exact position and depth.

hostile.q: Your contractor is experienced and insured. Why do you, as owner, insist on approving the logistics plan and the monitoring triggers?
hostile.a: Because the plan and the triggers decide the production rate and the safety of the neighbours and the street, and both land on me as owner if they fail. Approving them costs me a meeting. I am not taking over the contractor's means and methods; I am confirming that the contract's controls are in place, with a stop level and someone independent who can use it.
